title: Collecting, classifying and tabulating data
summary: Plan a fair collection, classify every observation consistently, and organise raw data into checked one-way and two-way frequency tables.
objectives: Distinguish categorical and quantitative data and identify suitable collection methods.
Create non-overlapping categories that include every valid observation.
Construct and check one-way and two-way frequency tables from raw data.

sections.title: Begin with a clear data question

blocks.text: Data are observations collected to answer a question. State the population you want to understand, the variable you will record and the unit or category before collecting anything. A population is the complete group of interest; a sample is the smaller group actually observed. A sample should represent the population rather than only the easiest people to reach.

Categorical data use labels such as travel method or preferred activity. Quantitative data use numbers. Counts such as the number of siblings are discrete because they take separate values, while measurements such as time or mass may vary continuously. This distinction guides the categories, units and table structure.

Categories must be mutually exclusive, so an observation cannot enter two categories, and exhaustive, so every valid observation has a place. For ages, intervals such as 10–12 and 12–14 overlap at 12. Use unambiguous boundaries such as 10 ≤ age < 12 and 12 ≤ age < 14, or list individual integer ages when that matches the question.

Read the raw list once and add one tally for each observation. Convert tallies to frequencies only after the list is complete. Then add every frequency and compare the sum with the number of observations. The visual example shows the complete route from raw travel methods to a checked frequency table.

sections.title: Worked example: construct a one-way table

prompt.text: Eight response times, in minutes, are 12, 9, 11, 12, 10, 9, 12 and 11. Construct a frequency table and identify the most frequent time.

content.text: List the distinct values in order: 9, 10, 11 and 12 minutes. This prevents a value from being omitted or counted in the wrong row.
Tally each entry, then convert the tallies to frequencies.
The greatest frequency is 3, so 12 minutes is the most frequent time.

sections.verification_note: The four frequencies total 8, matching the eight raw observations, and recounting the list confirms that 12 occurs three times.

sections.title: Worked example: complete a two-way table

prompt.text: Group A has 14 learners choosing reading and 11 choosing sport. Group B has 9 choosing reading and 16 choosing sport. Complete the row totals, column totals and grand total.

content.text: Find the grand total in two independent ways.
Record the margins around the four inner frequencies. A two-way table lets the reader compare one variable within levels of another variable without mixing the categories.

sections.verification_note: Both the row totals and the column totals give the same grand total of 50, so the completed margins are internally consistent.

sections.title: Collect data without building in bias

blocks.text: Use measurement for quantities such as height, observation for visible events and a questionnaire for opinions or self-reported behaviour. Record the same variable in the same way for every observation. A leading question such as ‘How useful was the excellent workshop?’ encourages a favourable response; a neutral version asks respondents to rate usefulness on a stated scale.

Missing responses, changing units and convenience samples can make a neat table unreliable. Keep an ‘other’ or ‘no response’ category when appropriate, state units in the heading, and describe who was sampled. Classification organises the evidence; it cannot repair a biased collection method.

prompt.text: A frequency table has category frequencies 7, 12, 5 and 6. What is the sample size?

feedback.text: Add every category frequency: 7 + 12 + 5 + 6 = 30. The total is the sample size represented by the table.

blocks.text: State the data question, population, variable and unit or categories. Use a collection method and sample that fit the question.
Make categories non-overlapping and complete, tally every observation once, and label rows and columns clearly.
Check a one-way table against the sample size. In a two-way table, confirm that row totals and column totals produce the same grand total.
